II17A-01.note: North-facing slopes are colder but get less UV, so darker beetles there fit heat but not UV; needs the hypothesis plus the final sentence. D is most tempting: it is consistent with Halloran but equally with Ide (the passage says both fit elevation), so it does not directly support her over him.

II17A-02.note: Potters dig clay locally, so Okrin-made ware should match Okrin beds and not coastal ones. B is the mirror (supports the trade account); D fails to discriminate. A and B form a reversed pair, which halves the field for a pattern-reader.

II17A-03.note: Inland bridges remove sea spray, so galvanized vs ungalvanized inland isolates the acid-cleaning factor. B is the strong distractor: galvanized coastal vs ungalvanized inland changes both variables at once, so it is confounded; A supports the consultant.

II17A-04.note: 'After every one of the southern plains' requires Sorrin to be fewer-cratered than the youngest southern plain, Dunmo (57, the lowest southern count). A uses Kettle, a northern plain, so it is irrelevant; C and D compare against older southern plains, which does not establish 'every one'.

II17A-05.note: Only 6h and 8h meet peak<20 and trough>4; the least frequent of those is 8h. B (12h) is the tempting near-miss but fails both limits (21 > 20, 3.1 < 4); A meets limits but is not least frequent.

II17A-06.note: Clay at ~85 m: P (22 m) is shallow, S (96 m) is deep, so A is the only shallow-vs-deep comparison. B is tempting because R fell only 1.3 m, but R's screen at 78 m is still above the clay, so B compares two shallow wells (and R's small drop is awkward data for the claim); C and D are within-aquifer.

II17B-01.note: The board heard only merchant-vs-merchant cases while the herring slump hit everyone, so merchant suits falling with craftsmen steady discriminates. A is tempting but inland towns lacked both the board and the herring trade, so it cannot separate the accounts; D supports the rivals; B is C reversed.

II17B-02.note: The horns are used in both settings but the veterans march only in processions, so equal slowing in seated concerts supports the horn account. B supports the archivist; D fails to discriminate because the horns (late 1920s) also came after 1919; C contradicts Lindqvist.

II17B-03.note: Carriage is charged by weight, so cheaper hauling should narrow gaps most for heavy grain, while a price bulletin should not favor heavy goods. A is the strong distractor: the bulletin riders also used the turnpikes, so turnpike towns being favored fits both accounts; B fits the bulletin; C is D reversed.

II17B-04.note: 'For children who already received the books, the lessons added little' = books-only (+8) vs books-and-lessons (+9). C shows the books' effect, not the lessons' marginal effect; D shows that books add a lot to lessons, which is the reverse conditional.

II17B-05.note: A larger proportion accepted needs submitted and accepted together: 30/120 (25%) to 120/240 (50%). C is tempting but gives accepted counts only, which a pure supply rise could also produce; B covers submissions only; D is about portraits.

II17B-06.note: The same individuals, aged 20-29 in 1995 and 45-54 in 2020, went from 38% to 40%, so they did not abandon the vowel as they aged. A is the strong distractor: it compares two different cohorts of 20-somethings (a change over time, not a change with aging); B and D are cross-sectional, which is the age gradient the skeptics rely on.
